analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give notice before electronically monitoring workers and limits workplace surveillance.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on September 16, 1992 with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set the first federal rules for employers who electronically monitor their employees, such as tracking computer work, counting phone calls, or watching video. It required posted and written notice about monitoring, let new workers be monitored more freely but sharply limited surveillance of workers with five or more years on the job, banned cameras in bathrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms, restricted using monitoring statistics as the sole basis for evaluations or quotas, and gave employees the right to see the data collected on them. It could be enforced through fines up to $10,000 per violation, Labor Department lawsuits, and private lawsuits by workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are monitored on the job, especially telephone and computer-monitored employees such as call-center staff, who would get advance notice of monitoring, access to the data collected on them, protection from hidden cameras and surveillance in private spaces, and the ability to sue. Prospective employees would learn about monitoring at their first interview, and customers would be told when their service calls are being observed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Monitored workers, call-center staff, job applicants

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to post a general notice that they engage in or may engage in electronic monitoring and to give workers prior written notice describing what will be monitored, when, and how the data will be used.

Bars employers from periodic or random electronic monitoring of workers with five or more cumulative years of employment, and bans monitoring in bathrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms except under a narrow suspicion-based exception requiring a signed, retained statement.

Prohibits using quantitative monitoring data as the sole basis for performance evaluations or production quotas, and bars taking action against an employee based on data collected in violation of the Act.

Gives employees the right to review personal data collected about them, restricts who the employer can disclose it to, and protects workers who file complaints from retaliation, with enforcement through civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation, Labor Department actions, and private lawsuits with attorney's fees.
Extends the same protections to employees of the House of Representatives and the Senate, applying the Act to Congress's own workplaces.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use electronic monitoring, who would bear the cost of notice, paperwork, recordkeeping, limits on how they manage and evaluate workers, civil fines up to $10,000 per violation, and litigation risk from private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes substantial compliance costs on employers, who must issue general and specific written notices, notify job applicants at first interviews, and even disclose telephone monitoring in advertisements and on customer bills.

By barring quantitative monitoring data as the sole basis for evaluations and quotas, the bill would make it harder for employers to manage productivity in heavily monitored jobs, which supporters of monitoring argue is a legitimate quality and performance tool.
The private right of action with attorney's fees and a three-year limitations period could expose employers to litigation over technical notice violations even where no worker was actually harmed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in monitored jobs, the bill offered real, concrete protections: notice, access to their own data, limits on hidden cameras and surveillance of private spaces, and a prohibition on quota-setting based purely on machine counts. The costs fall on employers in the form of compliance paperwork, some loss of flexibility in managing heavily monitored workforces, and litigation exposure. The core tradeoff is worker privacy and dignity against employer convenience and productivity management; the bill's carve-outs for law enforcement, national security, financial-sector compliance monitoring, and workers'-compensation investigations show an attempt to preserve legitimate uses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-September 1992, sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until Congress ended in early January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Simon introduced the Privacy for Consumers and Workers Act in the Senate on September 16, 1992.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use electronic monitoring are better off, because no federal notice requirements, data-use limits, or penalties were enacted. Workplace monitoring remained largely unregulated at the federal level.

for.name: Sen. Paul Simon
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of any party, so no meaningful partisan split ever developed in the record.

industries.industry: Call centers and telecom customer-service operations
industries.note: These employers rely heavily on telephone service observation and call accounting; the bill would have required advance notice, public disclosure in ads and bills, and limits on using call statistics as the sole basis for evaluations and quotas. Their interest in unrestricted monitoring ran against workers' privacy.

The bill imposed notice, recordkeeping, data-use, and disclosure requirements with fines up to $10,000 per violation and a private right of action. It would have ended unregulated surveillance of workers.

industries.industry: Congress as an employer (House and Senate employing authorities)
industries.note: The bill applied its monitoring rules and a $10,000-per-violation penalty to congressional employing offices. Incumbent officeholders' own workplaces would have been subject to the same rules they were asked to impose on private employers.
